analysis.one_liner: Requires police agencies to report misconduct settlements and judgments into a public Justice Department database.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee since its introduction with no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federal law enforcement agencies, and every state or local government that receives certain federal justice grants, to report each year how many misconduct lawsuits they settled or lost, what the cases alleged, what personnel actions followed, and how much money was paid and from what source. The Justice Department would publish everything in a searchable public database and report on ways agencies could reduce misconduct. Governments that refuse to report could lose up to 10% of two federal policing grant programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and residents gain visibility into who pays for police misconduct and out of which budgets — including the federal Judgment Fund, agency budgets, insurance, and bonds. Civil rights and police professional groups would be consulted on best practices, and researchers would get a national dataset.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities tracking police costs

how_it_helps.text: Federal law enforcement agencies must collect and report annually the number of misconduct judgments and settlements, the type of allegation (use of force, racial profiling, wrongful death, sexual assault, false testimony and more), personnel actions taken, total amounts paid, and the source of the money, including the federal Judgment Fund.

States and localities receiving Byrne JAG grants must report the same information and additionally disclose insurance premiums, bonds (with future interest and fees), and contributions to risk pools used to pay misconduct claims, and publish the data on their own websites.

The Attorney General must create and maintain a public, searchable database of all reported data within one year, with no personally identifiable officer information, and verify state and local submissions against open sources like court records and newspapers.

The Government Accountability Office would study the data after two years, identifying which agencies spend the most on misconduct judgments and settlements and recommending how agencies can reduce misconduct.

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies bear the cost of collecting and reporting the data. States or localities that fail to comply face a cut of up to 10% of their Byrne JAG or Cops on the Beat grant funding, with forfeited amounts redirected to complying governments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Police agencies and noncompliant grant recipients

drawbacks.text: The 10% funding penalty targets Byrne JAG and Cops on the Beat grants, which fund local crime prevention and policing programs; jurisdictions losing that money could see reduced public-safety services.

The bill only covers misconduct that ends in a judgment or settlement — allegations resolved without payment, or conduct never sued over, would never appear in the database, so it measures costs rather than the full scope of misconduct.
Reporting alone does not change officer conduct or agency discipline; the bill's only teeth are data collection and a study, with recommendations rather than mandates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: taxpayers currently pay hundreds of millions in police misconduct settlements with little public accounting of where the money comes from, and this bill would make that visible. The costs are modest — agency paperwork and a possible grant cut for governments that refuse to report. The honest limitation is that transparency does not by itself reduce misconduct; the bill bets that public data and a GAO study will create pressure for change.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late January 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it has received no further action.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Kaine introduced the bill in the Senate on January 29, 2026.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary, and no markup, hearing, or vote has followed.
No senator has cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has been forced to change anything: law enforcement agencies face no new disclosure requirements, and the status quo — misconduct settlements paid with limited public accounting — continues while the bill sits without a committee vote.

for.name: Tim Kaine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cost of Police Misconduct Act of 2026 in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; no markup, hearing, or vote scheduled
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and has taken no further action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred. The bill has a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and sits in a committee chaired by a Republican, so no partisan pattern can be read from the record yet.

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, and local)
industries.note: The bill would require them to disclose misconduct judgments, settlements, and payment sources publicly, and expose noncompliant grant recipients to a funding cut. Keeping these costs out of public view is the status quo they benefit from, while taxpayers foot the settlements.

industries.industry: Government liability insurers and risk pools
industries.note: State and local governments would have to disclose insurance premiums, bonds, and risk-pool contributions used to pay misconduct claims, shining light on how liability costs are financed. This is a disclosure burden rather than a direct financial hit.

industries.industry: Police professional associations (FOP, IACP, NOBLE and others)
industries.note: The bill directs the Attorney General to develop best practices in consultation with named law enforcement associations alongside civil rights groups, giving them a formal seat in the process.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, a Republican Senate majority, and no committee action more than a year before the Congress ends, the bill is very unlikely to get a markup or floor vote unless policing transparency suddenly becomes a legislative priority. Its most probable fate is expiring quietly in committee at the end of the 119th Congress.
